Tools by server (class, duration in cycles, price):
- iot, with site_name MAIN and asset_id hyd_1: sites, asset_ids, assets, asset_detail, installed_sensors, measured_sensors, find_assets_by_sensors, stream_extent and sensor_coverage (read, 0, free) describe the registry and the recorded stream. history(site_name, asset_id, start, end, sensors, limit, cursor) (read, the cycles it plays, price per cycle by group) returns the recorded rows of a window, and latest_reading(site_name, asset_id, sensor) (read, 0, price per cycle by group) returns the newest recorded row.
- fmsr: get_failure_modes(asset_class) (read, 0, free) returns the failure mode codes of a component class, cooler, valve, pump or accumulator, with their source.
- wo, with site_id MAIN: list_workorders, get_workorder, get_workorder_tasks, get_workorder_costs, get_workorder_actuals_vs_planned, get_workorder_kpis, get_schedule_calendar, get_my_assigned_workorders and get_failure_codes (read, 0, free) read the work orders of this episode and the failure code catalog. generate_work_order(description, asset_num, site_id, priority, work_type, reported_by, location, notes, wonum, aob_source) (write, 0, part price plus the repair charge of 20, plus a visit charge of 15 for the order that opens a visit) asks a technician to restore the component of a child asset to its healthy level, with work_type CM and an empty wonum, since the environment numbers the orders wo-1 and up, and aob_source an object with the prediction_id and the evidence_ids behind the order. With work_type EM the order is an emergency order, which forms a visit of its own, arrives 1 cycle after its creation at 2.0 times the part and repair price, and holds the component at its healthy level for 10 cycles after its close. A component that an emergency order still holds when the episode ends is scored at the level it had before that order. Parts: cooler 20, valve 20, pump 30, accumulator 20. The technician arrives after the lead time and repairs while the rig stands still, then the order closes. Lead times: cooler 3, valve 3, pump 3, accumulator 3. Repair downtimes: cooler 1, valve 1, pump 2, accumulator 1. A work order is refused before a diagnosis or a declaration, and while an order on the same component is open. An order on a healthy component is executed and counted as unnecessary.
- task: get_asset_profile() (read, 0, free) returns these rules, the child assets, the normal ranges of the channel means under the record fields and the tool table.
  submit_diagnosis(cooler, valve, pump, accumulator, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records one condition level per component, accepted once and never after a declaration. A wrong diagnosis costs the misdiagnosis price of 15, the call-out that it wastes. The price is added to the cost of the episode when the episode is scored and does not fall from the budget. declare_insufficient_evidence(sensor_group, cycles, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records that the evidence cannot separate the remaining candidates and names the reading that would, accepted once and never after a diagnosis, and work orders stay allowed afterward. It must cite at least one reading already read, and a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure. finish(summary) (write, 0, free) ends the episode. With no further call the rig then runs until the open work orders close while the downtime accrues, and the episode is scored after the last close.
evidence_ids of the task tools is a comma separated list of identifiers, possibly empty, and aob_source.evidence_ids a list of them: obs/<timestamp>/<field> for a value of a telemetry row, with the timestamp and the field as the row shows them, wo/<wonum> for a work order, fmea/<source>/<code> for a failure mode and alarm/<cycle>/<channel> for the alarm of a notification. aob_source.prediction_id is empty in this episode.
Every answer ends with one JSON line with the price of the call, the budget left, the steps left, the cycle and the notifications since the previous call of the work orders executed and closed, the alarms of the sensor groups already read and the failures, then the end of the episode. An alarm is raised once per channel in an episode, so a channel that leaves its normal range again after a repair raises no second alarm, and only a new reading of the telemetry shows it.

Downtime accrues per cycle while a component is below its healthy level (cooler: level 100 0, level 20 1, level 3 2; valve: level 100 0, level 90 1, level 80 2, level 73 3; pump: level 0 0, level 1 1, level 2 2; accumulator: level 130 0, level 115 1, level 100 2, level 90 3) and counts toward the cost of the episode, while the budget limits the prices alone. Budget: 300. Horizon: 60 cycles. Step cap: 60 tool calls, refused ones included. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode. Time advances only inside tool calls, by their declared durations. The episode ends on finish, at the horizon, at the step cap, after 1800 seconds of wall time, or when an action would exceed the budget; a component at its worst level for 10 cycles is a failure that adds 50 to the cost, and only a repair on it that has closed by then averts it. If the wall limit ends the episode while every call is answered or while your reply is being written, the episode ends there and is scored. A refused call costs nothing but counts as a step, and a call with a missing argument or an argument of the wrong type is refused.

Evidence rows carry the identifiers obs/<timestamp>/<field>; a channel mean outside its public normal range is marked NO in the column in normal range, and rows you have planned on collapse to one summary row per sensor group with the identifiers outside their normal range. A normal range spans the smallest to the largest mean of the channel over the stable recordings of the healthy rig, so a healthy rig shows no channel mean outside its normal range, while a fault usually shows at least one. The fix history lists the repairs recorded before the episode. The CausalDiagnosis MCP does not run on this row, so no ranking, advice or prediction exists: you form the candidates yourself. The failure modes table lists the failure modes the asset serves with their identifiers fmea/<source>/<code>, and their level, severity, recommended action and indicating channels where this row gives them. Channels outside their normal range shows, for every sensor group read, its latest cycle with the channel means outside their normal ranges, below or above. Your candidates lists the combinations of your latest plan that listed them, in your order. Refuted repair plans list the component sets whose verification on the normal ranges failed. The timeline lists alarms (alarm/<t>/<channel>) and closed work orders (wo/<id>).

Step kinds. Three kinds read the opening, each free. profile, no args, reads the asset profile and comes first, since the board holds nothing about the asset before it. failure_modes, args {"component": <a component, or "" for every component>}, reads the failure modes the asset serves. fix_history, no args, reads the repairs recorded before the episode. Four kinds act on the rig: read, diagnose, declare and order. A sixth, finish, ends the episode, and a seventh, recall, brings collapsed readings back to the board.
- read: args {"sensor_group": <group>, "cycles": <n>}; expect {"outside": [<the channel means your followed candidate pushes outside their normal ranges, each by its field name or its tag such as PS1>]}. After the reading, a listed channel that the reading served within its normal range is a surprise. A read of a group whose recorded cycles are all read already is not made and comes back as a surprise, since it would show nothing new; on a row whose clock runs, the record grows as the clock moves. Consecutive read steps of one plan run as one batch: the controller makes the reads one after the other and checks every expectation after the last, so a batch pays for all of its reads before it sees any of them. The schedule on the board, when one is shown, lists the reads that several of your candidates share, each once with the candidates it serves, and after a refuted plan what each remaining candidate still needs.
- diagnose: args {"rank": <rank in your candidates>}; no expectation. The controller submits the full combination of that candidate, the components it leaves out at their healthy level, with the evidence you cite and the channel means outside their normal ranges.
- declare: args {"sensor_group": <the group you would read next to separate your candidates>, "cycles": <n>}; no expectation. It must follow a reading, which the controller cites, since a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure.
- order: args {"component": <one component>}; no expectation, since no prediction exists on this row. The controller places the order after a diagnosis or a declaration only. One component per order step: a step that joins several names is split into one order per component, which count against the step limit.
The orders of one plan form one repair plan: once its last order has closed and no other order of yours is open, plan a read, and on the first reading at or after the close the controller verifies the repair plan on the normal ranges, which judge the whole rig. It is refuted when any channel mean of that reading lies outside its normal range: the controller records its component set and marks it on the board, and you repair another candidate.
- finish: no args and no expectation. The controller writes the closing summary and ends the episode.
- recall: args {"sensor_group": <a group>, "observations": [<first>, <last>]}; no expectation. It calls no tool and costs nothing: the controller puts the full rows of that group's observations first to last, which the board collapsed into a summary row, back on the next board, once. A plan of recalls alone makes no call and still takes one step.
Every step carries "evidence": a list of the identifiers from the board that justify it, the few that moved you, and only identifiers that appear on the board.

With work_type EM the order is an emergency order, which forms a visit of its own, arrives 1 cycle after its creation at 2.0 times the part and repair price, and holds the component at its healthy level for 10 cycles after its close. A component that an emergency order still holds when the episode ends is scored at the level it had before that order. Parts: cooler 20, valve 20, pump 30, accumulator 20. The technician arrives after the lead time and repairs while the rig stands still, then the order closes. Lead times: cooler 3, valve 3, pump 3, accumulator 3. Repair downtimes: cooler 1, valve 1, pump 2, accumulator 1. A work order is refused before a diagnosis or a declaration, and while an order on the same component is open. An order on a healthy component is executed and counted as unnecessary.
- task: get_asset_profile() (read, 0, free) returns these rules, the child assets, the normal ranges of the channel means under the record fields and the tool table.
  submit_diagnosis(cooler, valve, pump, accumulator, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records one condition level per component, accepted once and never after a declaration. A wrong diagnosis costs the misdiagnosis price of 15, the call-out that it wastes. The price is added to the cost of the episode when the episode is scored and does not fall from the budget. declare_insufficient_evidence(sensor_group, cycles, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records that the evidence cannot separate the remaining candidates and names the reading that would, accepted once and never after a diagnosis, and work orders stay allowed afterward. It must cite at least one reading already read, and a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure. finish(summary) (write, 0, free) ends the episode. With no further call the rig then runs until the open work orders close while the downtime accrues, and the episode is scored after the last close.
evidence_ids of the task tools is a comma separated list of identifiers, possibly empty, and aob_source.evidence_ids a list of them: obs/<timestamp>/<field> for a value of a telemetry row, with the timestamp and the field as the row shows them, wo/<wonum> for a work order, fmea/<source>/<code> for a failure mode and alarm/<cycle>/<channel> for the alarm of a notification. aob_source.prediction_id is empty in this episode.
Every answer ends with one JSON line with the price of the call, the budget left, the steps left, the cycle and the notifications since the previous call of the work orders executed and closed, the alarms of the sensor groups already read and the failures, then the end of the episode. An alarm is raised once per channel in an episode, so a channel that leaves its normal range again after a repair raises no second alarm, and only a new reading of the telemetry shows it.

Downtime accrues per cycle while a component is below its healthy level (cooler: level 100 0, level 20 1, level 3 2; valve: level 100 0, level 90 1, level 80 2, level 73 3; pump: level 0 0, level 1 1, level 2 2; accumulator: level 130 0, level 115 1, level 100 2, level 90 3) and counts toward the cost of the episode, while the budget limits the prices alone. Budget: 300. Horizon: 60 cycles. Step cap: 60 tool calls, refused ones included. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode. Time advances only inside tool calls, by their declared durations. The episode ends on finish, at the horizon, at the step cap, after 1800 seconds of wall time, or when an action would exceed the budget; a component at its worst level for 10 cycles is a failure that adds 50 to the cost, and only a repair on it that has closed by then averts it. If the wall limit ends the episode while every call is answered or while your reply is being written, the episode ends there and is scored. A refused call costs nothing but counts as a step, and a call with a missing argument or an argument of the wrong type is refused.

Step kinds. Three kinds read the opening, each free. profile, no args, reads the asset profile and comes first, since the board holds nothing about the asset before it. failure_modes, args {"component": <a component, or "" for every component>}, reads the failure modes the asset serves. fix_history, no args, reads the repairs recorded before the episode. Four kinds act on the rig: read, diagnose, declare and order. A sixth, finish, ends the episode, and a seventh, recall, brings collapsed readings back to the board.
- read: args {"sensor_group": <group>, "cycles": <n>}; expect {"outside": [<the channel means your followed candidate pushes outside their normal ranges, each by its field name or its tag such as PS1>]}. After the reading, a listed channel that the reading served within its normal range is a surprise. A read of a group whose recorded cycles are all read already is not made and comes back as a surprise, since it would show nothing new; on a row whose clock runs, the record grows as the clock moves. Consecutive read steps of one plan run as one batch: the controller makes the reads one after the other and checks every expectation after the last, so a batch pays for all of its reads before it sees any of them. The schedule on the board, when one is shown, lists the reads that several of your candidates share, each once with the candidates it serves, and after a refuted plan what each remaining candidate still needs.
- diagnose: args {"rank": <rank in your candidates>}; no expectation. The controller submits the full combination of that candidate, the components it leaves out at their healthy level, with the evidence you cite and the channel means outside their normal ranges.
- declare: args {"sensor_group": <the group you would read next to separate your candidates>, "cycles": <n>}; no expectation. It must follow a reading, which the controller cites, since a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure.
- order: args {"component": <one component>}; no expectation, since no prediction exists on this row. The controller places the order after a diagnosis or a declaration only. The orders of one plan form one repair plan: once its last order has closed and no other order of yours is open, plan a read, and on the first reading at or after the close the controller verifies the repair plan on the normal ranges, which judge the whole rig. It is refuted when any channel mean of that reading lies outside its normal range: the controller records its component set and marks it on the board, and you repair another candidate.
- finish: no args and no expectation. The controller writes the closing summary and ends the episode.
- recall: args {"sensor_group": <a group>, "observations": [<first>, <last>]}; no expectation. It calls no tool and costs nothing: the controller puts the full rows of that group's observations first to last, which the board collapsed into a summary row, back on the next board, once. A plan of recalls alone makes no call and still takes one step.

The why line names the failure mode identifiers or the readings that moved you. You never write a probability, since no mass exists on this row.

The controller refuses a plan whatever you write only where the environment or the plan itself would fail: the opening comes first, the profile before the rest; no diagnosis without your candidates; no work order without a prior diagnosis or declaration; no declaration before a reading it can cite; no finish before the reading that verifies the last repair plan, unless the budget, the horizon or the step cap leaves no room for it; no plan that the budget, the horizon or the step cap cannot pay. The controller executes your steps while every expectation holds and calls you again only when one fails, with the surprise written on the board, so plan several steps and attach an expectation you are willing to be stopped by. A plan the controller cannot parse or refuses runs nothing, and you are asked again with its reasons; so is a differential the controller cannot parse. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode.

Exactly one diagnosis or one declaration of insufficient evidence is allowed per episode, a work order needs a prior diagnosis or declaration, and the episode ends with finish or when a limit of its row ends it: the horizon, the step cap, the budget, the limit of wall time or a component failure, each where the row sets it. Each turn you receive the board and return one JSON object, with nothing after it.

The board. Before the profile is read it holds nothing about the rig and names the reads of the opening. Evidence rows carry the identifiers obs/<timestamp>/<field>; a channel mean outside its public normal range is marked NO in the column in normal range, and rows you have planned on collapse to one summary row per sensor group with the identifiers outside their normal range. A normal range spans the smallest to the largest mean of the channel over the stable recordings of the healthy rig, so a healthy rig shows no channel mean outside its normal range, while a fault usually shows at least one. The fix history lists the repairs recorded before the episode. The CausalDiagnosis MCP does not run on this row, so no ranking, advice or prediction exists: you form the candidates yourself. The failure modes table lists the failure modes the asset serves with their identifiers fmea/<source>/<code>, and their level, severity, recommended action and indicating channels where this row gives them. Channels outside their normal range shows, for every sensor group read, its latest cycle with the channel means outside their normal ranges, below or above. Your candidates lists the combinations of your latest plan that listed them, in your order. Refuted repair plans list the component sets whose verification on the normal ranges failed. The timeline lists alarms (alarm/<t>/<channel>) and closed work orders (wo/<id>).

Step kinds. Three kinds read the opening, each free. profile, no args, reads the asset profile and comes first, since the board holds nothing about the asset before it. failure_modes, args {"component": <a component, or "" for every component>}, reads the failure modes the asset serves. fix_history, no args, reads the repairs recorded before the episode. Four kinds act on the rig: read, diagnose, declare and order. A sixth, finish, ends the episode, and a seventh, recall, brings collapsed readings back to the board.
- read: args {"sensor_group": <group>, "cycles": <n>}; expect {"outside": [<the channel means your followed candidate pushes outside their normal ranges, each by its field name or its tag such as PS1>]}. After the reading, a listed channel that the reading served within its normal range is a surprise. A read of a group whose recorded cycles are all read already is not made and comes back as a surprise, since it would show nothing new; on a row whose clock runs, the record grows as the clock moves. Consecutive read steps of one plan run as one batch: the controller makes the reads one after the other and checks every expectation after the last, so a batch pays for all of its reads before it sees any of them. The schedule on the board, when one is shown, lists the reads that several of your candidates share, each once with the candidates it serves, and after a refuted plan what each remaining candidate still needs.
- diagnose: args {"rank": <rank in your candidates>}; no expectation. The controller submits the full combination of that candidate, the components it leaves out at their healthy level, with the evidence you cite and the channel means outside their normal ranges.
- declare: args {"sensor_group": <the group you would read next to separate your candidates>, "cycles": <n>}; no expectation. It must follow a reading, which the controller cites, since a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure.
- order: args {"component": <one component>}; no expectation, since no prediction exists on this row. The controller places the order after a diagnosis or a declaration only. One component per order step: a step that joins several names is split into one order per component, which count against the step limit.
The orders of one plan form one repair plan: once its last order has closed and no other order of yours is open, plan a read, and on the first reading at or after the close the controller verifies the repair plan on the normal ranges, which judge the whole rig. It is refuted when any channel mean of that reading lies outside its normal range: the controller records its component set and marks it on the board, and you repair another candidate.
- finish: no args and no expectation. The controller writes the closing summary and ends the episode.
- recall: args {"sensor_group": <a group>, "observations": [<first>, <last>]}; no expectation. It calls no tool and costs nothing: the controller puts the full rows of that group's observations first to last, which the board collapsed into a summary row, back on the next board, once. A plan of recalls alone makes no call and still takes one step.
Every step carries "evidence": a list of the identifiers from the board that justify it, the few that moved you, and only identifiers that appear on the board.
On this row the controller calls AssetOpsBench's servers for the kinds: read calls history of the iot server over the newest recorded cycles the group has not paid for, with the group's sensors and their _std fields; order calls generate_work_order of the wo server on the child asset of the component, with work_type CM and the prediction and the evidence in aob_source; diagnose, declare and finish call the task server. Time passes with your thinking on this row, which serves no wait: a history window past the present plays the cycles it reaches where reads take time, and a work order closes after its lead time and downtime. The failure modes come from get_failure_modes of the fmsr server and the fix history from list_workorders of the wo server. One more kind of the opening exists on this row, after the profile, and a reading needs it first: extent, no args, the extent of the record by stream_extent of the iot server.

The plan. Return
{"branch": <rank of the candidate you follow in your candidates>, "mode": "test_first" | "act_now" | "repair_as_test" | "declare", "why": "<one line>", "candidates": [{"levels": {"<component>": <level>, ...}, "failure_mode_ids": ["fmea/<source>/<code>", ...]}, ...], "steps": [{"kind": ..., "args": {...}, "expect": {...}, "evidence": [...]}, ...]}
with as many entries under steps as the budget, the horizon and the step cap pay, finish included, and candidates best first; a plan they cannot pay is refused and you are asked again. A candidate names the faulty components at levels of the profile, every other component staying at its healthy level, and a candidate with no faulty component states a healthy unit. candidates is needed before your first diagnosis and may be left out later, when the board keeps your last list. test_first reads to separate your candidates and commits when the readings support one; act_now diagnoses and orders the faulty components of the candidate you follow, then reads after the close so that the controller verifies; repair_as_test orders the cheapest repair of a likely candidate when no affordable reading separates it; declare names a sensor group when no reading you can afford would separate your candidates. The why line names the failure mode identifiers or the readings that moved you. You never write a probability, since no mass exists on this row.

The controller refuses a plan whatever you write only where the environment or the plan itself would fail: the opening comes first, the profile before the rest; no diagnosis without your candidates; no work order without a prior diagnosis or declaration; no declaration before a reading it can cite; no finish before the reading that verifies the last repair plan, unless the budget, the horizon or the step cap leaves no room for it; no plan that the budget, the horizon or the step cap cannot pay. The controller executes your steps while every expectation holds and calls you again only when one fails, with the surprise written on the board, so plan several steps and attach an expectation you are willing to be stopped by. A plan the controller cannot parse or refuses runs nothing, and you are asked again with its reasons; so is a differential the controller cannot parse. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode.

With no further call the rig then runs until the open work orders close while the downtime accrues, and the episode is scored after the last close.
evidence_ids of the task tools is a comma separated list of identifiers, possibly empty, and aob_source.evidence_ids a list of them: obs/<timestamp>/<field> for a value of a telemetry row, with the timestamp and the field as the row shows them, wo/<wonum> for a work order, fmea/<source>/<code> for a failure mode and alarm/<cycle>/<channel> for the alarm of a notification. aob_source.prediction_id is empty in this episode.
Every answer ends with one JSON line with the price of the call, the budget left, the steps left, the cycle and the notifications since the previous call of the work orders executed and closed, the alarms of the sensor groups already read and the failures, then the end of the episode. An alarm is raised once per channel in an episode, so a channel that leaves its normal range again after a repair raises no second alarm, and only a new reading of the telemetry shows it.

Downtime accrues per cycle while a component is below its healthy level (cooler: level 100 0, level 20 1, level 3 2; valve: level 100 0, level 90 1, level 80 2, level 73 3; pump: level 0 0, level 1 1, level 2 2; accumulator: level 130 0, level 115 1, level 100 2, level 90 3) and counts toward the cost of the episode, while the budget limits the prices alone. Budget: 300. Horizon: 60 cycles. Step cap: 60 tool calls, refused ones included. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode. Time advances only inside tool calls, by their declared durations. The episode ends on finish, at the horizon, at the step cap, after 1800 seconds of wall time, or when an action would exceed the budget; a component at its worst level for 10 cycles is a failure that adds 50 to the cost, and only a repair on it that has closed by then averts it. If the wall limit ends the episode while every call is answered or while your reply is being written, the episode ends there and is scored. A refused call costs nothing but counts as a step, and a call with a missing argument or an argument of the wrong type is refused.

evidence_ids of the task tools is a comma separated list of identifiers, possibly empty, and aob_source.evidence_ids a list of them: obs/<timestamp>/<field> for a value of a telemetry row, with the timestamp and the field as the row shows them, wo/<wonum> for a work order, fmea/<source>/<code> for a failure mode and alarm/<cycle>/<channel> for the alarm of a notification. aob_source.prediction_id is empty in this episode.

An alarm is raised once per channel in an episode, so a channel that leaves its normal range again after a repair raises no second alarm, and only a new reading of the telemetry shows it.

Downtime accrues per cycle while a component is below its healthy level (cooler: level 100 0, level 20 1, level 3 2; valve: level 100 0, level 90 1, level 80 2, level 73 3; pump: level 0 0, level 1 1, level 2 2; accumulator: level 130 0, level 115 1, level 100 2, level 90 3) and counts toward the cost of the episode, while the budget limits the prices alone. Budget: 300. Horizon: 60 cycles. Step cap: 60 tool calls, refused ones included. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode. Time advances only inside tool calls, by their declared durations. The episode ends on finish, at the horizon, at the step cap, after 1800 seconds of wall time, or when an action would exceed the budget; a component at its worst level for 10 cycles is a failure that adds 50 to the cost, and only a repair on it that has closed by then averts it. If the wall limit ends the episode while every call is answered or while your reply is being written, the episode ends there and is scored. A refused call costs nothing but counts as a step, and a call with a missing argument or an argument of the wrong type is refused.

A normal range spans the smallest to the largest mean of the channel over the stable recordings of the healthy rig, so a healthy rig shows no channel mean outside its normal range, while a fault usually shows at least one. Step kinds. Three kinds read the opening, each free. profile, no args, reads the asset profile and comes first, since the board holds nothing about the asset before it. failure_modes, args {"component": <a component, or "" for every component>}, reads the failure modes the asset serves. fix_history, no args, reads the repairs recorded before the episode. Four kinds act on the rig: read, diagnose, declare and order. A sixth, finish, ends the episode, and a seventh, recall, brings collapsed readings back to the board.
- read: args {"sensor_group": <group>, "cycles": <n>}; expect {"outside": [<the channel means your followed candidate pushes outside their normal ranges, each by its field name or its tag such as PS1>]}. After the reading, a listed channel that the reading served within its normal range is a surprise. A read of a group whose recorded cycles are all read already is not made and comes back as a surprise, since it would show nothing new; on a row whose clock runs, the record grows as the clock moves. Consecutive read steps of one plan run as one batch: the controller makes the reads one after the other and checks every expectation after the last, so a batch pays for all of its reads before it sees any of them. The schedule on the board, when one is shown, lists the reads that several of your candidates share, each once with the candidates it serves, and after a refuted plan what each remaining candidate still needs.
- diagnose: args {"rank": <rank in your candidates>}; no expectation. The controller submits the full combination of that candidate, the components it leaves out at their healthy level, with the evidence you cite and the channel means outside their normal ranges.
- declare: args {"sensor_group": <the group you would read next to separate your candidates>, "cycles": <n>}; no expectation. It must follow a reading, which the controller cites, since a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure.
- order: args {"component": <one component>}; no expectation, since no prediction exists on this row. The controller places the order after a diagnosis or a declaration only. One component per order step: a step that joins several names is split into one order per component, which count against the step limit.
The orders of one plan form one repair plan: once its last order has closed and no other order of yours is open, plan a read, and on the first reading at or after the close the controller verifies the repair plan on the normal ranges, which judge the whole rig. It is refuted when any channel mean of that reading lies outside its normal range: the controller records its component set and marks it on the board, and you repair another candidate.
- finish: no args and no expectation. The controller writes the closing summary and ends the episode.
- recall: args {"sensor_group": <a group>, "observations": [<first>, <last>]}; no expectation. It calls no tool and costs nothing: the controller puts the full rows of that group's observations first to last, which the board collapsed into a summary row, back on the next board, once. A plan of recalls alone makes no call and still takes one step.
Every step carries "evidence": a list of the identifiers from the board that justify it, the few that moved you, and only identifiers that appear on the board.

The why line names the failure mode identifiers or the readings that moved you. You never write a probability, since no mass exists on this row.

The controller refuses a plan whatever you write only where the environment or the plan itself would fail: the opening comes first, the profile before the rest; no diagnosis without your candidates; no work order without a prior diagnosis or declaration; no declaration before a reading it can cite; no finish before the reading that verifies the last repair plan, unless the budget, the horizon or the step cap leaves no room for it; no plan that the budget, the horizon or the step cap cannot pay. The controller executes your steps while every expectation holds and calls you again only when one fails, with the surprise written on the board, so plan several steps and attach an expectation you are willing to be stopped by. A plan the controller cannot parse or refuses runs nothing, and you are asked again with its reasons; so is a differential the controller cannot parse. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode.

Tools by server (class, duration in cycles, price):
- iot, with site_name MAIN and asset_id hyd_1: sites, asset_ids, assets, asset_detail, installed_sensors, measured_sensors, find_assets_by_sensors, stream_extent and sensor_coverage (read, 0, free) describe the registry and the recorded stream. history(site_name, asset_id, start, end, sensors, limit, cursor) (read, the cycles it plays, price per cycle by group) returns the recorded rows of a window, and latest_reading(site_name, asset_id, sensor) (read, 0, price per cycle by group) returns the newest recorded row.
- fmsr: get_failure_modes(asset_class) (read, 0, free) returns the failure mode codes of a component class, cooler, valve, pump or accumulator, with their source.
- wo, with site_id MAIN: list_workorders, get_workorder, get_workorder_tasks, get_workorder_costs, get_workorder_actuals_vs_planned, get_workorder_kpis, get_schedule_calendar, get_my_assigned_workorders and get_failure_codes (read, 0, free) read the work orders of this episode and the failure code catalog. generate_work_order(description, asset_num, site_id, priority, work_type, reported_by, location, notes, wonum, aob_source) (write, 0, part price plus the repair charge of 20, plus a visit charge of 15 for the order that opens a visit) asks a technician to restore the component of a child asset to its healthy level, with work_type CM and an empty wonum, since the environment numbers the orders wo-1 and up, and aob_source an object with the prediction_id and the evidence_ids behind the order. With work_type EM the order is an emergency order, which forms a visit of its own, arrives 1 cycle after its creation at 2.0 times the part and repair price, and holds the component at its healthy level for 10 cycles after its close. A component that an emergency order still holds when the episode ends is scored at the level it had before that order. Parts: cooler 20, valve 20, pump 30, accumulator 20. The technician arrives after the lead time and repairs while the rig stands still, then the order closes. Lead times: cooler 3, valve 3, pump 3, accumulator 3. Repair downtimes: cooler 1, valve 1, pump 2, accumulator 1. A work order is refused before a diagnosis or a declaration, and while an order on the same component is open. An order on a healthy component is executed and counted as unnecessary.
- task: get_asset_profile() (read, 0, free) returns these rules, the child assets, the normal ranges of the channel means under the record fields and the tool table.
  submit_diagnosis(cooler, valve, pump, accumulator, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records one condition level per component, accepted once and never after a declaration. A wrong diagnosis costs the misdiagnosis price of 15, the call-out that it wastes. The price is added to the cost of the episode when the episode is scored and does not fall from the budget. declare_insufficient_evidence(sensor_group, cycles, evidence_ids) (write, 0, free) records that the evidence cannot separate the remaining candidates and names the reading that would, accepted once and never after a diagnosis, and work orders stay allowed afterward. It must cite at least one reading already read, and a declaration that cites none is scored as a failure. finish(summary) (write, 0, free) ends the episode. With no further call the rig then runs until the open work orders close while the downtime accrues, and the episode is scored after the last close.
evidence_ids of the task tools is a comma separated list of identifiers, possibly empty, and aob_source.evidence_ids a list of them: obs/<timestamp>/<field> for a value of a telemetry row, with the timestamp and the field as the row shows them, wo/<wonum> for a work order, fmea/<source>/<code> for a failure mode and alarm/<cycle>/<channel> for the alarm of a notification. aob_source.prediction_id is empty in this episode.
Every answer ends with one JSON line with the price of the call, the budget left, the steps left, the cycle and the notifications since the previous call of the work orders executed and closed, the alarms of the sensor groups already read and the failures, then the end of the episode. An alarm is raised once per channel in an episode, so a channel that leaves its normal range again after a repair raises no second alarm, and only a new reading of the telemetry shows it.

Downtime accrues per cycle while a component is below its healthy level (cooler: level 100 0, level 20 1, level 3 2; valve: level 100 0, level 90 1, level 80 2, level 73 3; pump: level 0 0, level 1 1, level 2 2; accumulator: level 130 0, level 115 1, level 100 2, level 90 3) and counts toward the cost of the episode, while the budget limits the prices alone. Budget: 300. Horizon: 60 cycles. Step cap: 60 tool calls, refused ones included. A turn that calls no tool of the rig still takes one step, and as many requests in a row without a call as the step cap allows end the episode. Time advances only inside tool calls, by their declared durations. The episode ends on finish, at the horizon, at the step cap, after 1800 seconds of wall time, or when an action would exceed the budget; a component at its worst level for 10 cycles is a failure that adds 50 to the cost, and only a repair on it that has closed by then averts it. If the wall limit ends the episode while every call is answered or while your reply is being written, the episode ends there and is scored. A refused call costs nothing but counts as a step, and a call with a missing argument or an argument of the wrong type is refused.
